prompt.context: Our client is a regional electricity monopoly. Due to regulation, its market will be opened to competition next year on January 1. There are no actual competitors at this time; however, the client would like ideas on actions to take in the short-term in order to better prepare for potential competitors. They have no control over pricing and cost-cutting during this time period.
prompt.question: What actions should Central Power take in the short-term to prepare for the entry of potential competitors into its market?

clarifying_info.q: Do we know of any potential competitors?
clarifying_info.a: None at this time. Central Power is facing the threat of market entry.

clarifying_info.q: Do you have any information on pricing?
clarifying_info.a: Not really; pricing is controlled by the government, so it is beyond our control and will be the same for any competition.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other markets Central Power can enter?
clarifying_info.a: None at this time. Our engagement is focused on their home market.
Central Power has three divisions: (1) Sales and General Administration, (2) Generation and Transmission, (3) Maintenance and Repair.

clarifying_info.q: How many employees are in sales?
Does sales/customer service treat certain customer segments differently?
If there is a power outage, does Maintenance and Repair fix industrial clients first?
clarifying_info.a: No, they dispatch in the order of the call they receive.

clarifying_info.q: Has Central Power ever advertised or had a marketing campaign?
Is Central Power undertaking any capital investment?

exhibits.title: Revenue 2007
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down 2007 revenue and customer counts across three segments (Industrial, Commercial, Residential), plus a Historic Revenue line chart.

framework: Barriers to Entry: no external barriers possible (government deregulating); focus on internal barriers such as increasing switching costs and improving commercial attractiveness
Anticipation of Competitive Attack: use customer value data to predict which segment a rational competitor would target first, then pre-empt
Market Information: analyze revenue by segment and revenue per customer to identify where value is concentrated

Customer Retention Initiatives: systematically examine each division (Sales & General Admin, Generation & Transmission, Maintenance & Repair) for ways to deepen customer relationships and raise switching costs
Stakeholder Reaction: consider how employees, unions, and local government will respond to proposed changes

questions.prompt: Phase 1 — What is your reaction to Exhibit 1? What does the data tell you about the customer segments?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates immediately notice the disparity in revenue per customer across segments. Industrial customers are 150 in number but generate $150 MM (58% of total revenue). Commercial customers are 10,000 and generate $60 MM (23%). Residential customers are 100,000 and generate $48 MM (19%). The key insight is that industrial customers are disproportionately valuable and would be the primary target for any rational new entrant. Historical revenue trends are driven by population and government-set prices — both outside the company's control — so candidates should not focus on them.

math.setup: Calculate revenue per customer and share of total revenue for each segment. Total revenue = $150 MM + $60 MM + $48 MM = $258 MM.
steps: Residential Customer Equivalents of one Industrial customer: $1,000,000 / $480 ≈ 2,083 residential customers
Residential Customer Equivalents of one Commercial customer: $6,000 / $480 ≈ 13 residential customers
math.answer: Industrial customers generate ~$1 MM each (2,083x a residential customer); Commercial customers generate ~$6,000 each (13x a residential customer). Industrial segment = 58% of total revenue from only 150 customers.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 — Based on the data, if you were a competitor entering this market, which segment would you target? What should Central Power do to pre-empt this?
questions.guidance: Candidates should identify industrial customers as the competitor's primary target (highest revenue per customer, concentrated and easy to approach as a B2B segment). Central Power should bias all retention initiatives toward industrial and commercial customers. Candidates should then walk through each division of the company to generate specific retention ideas conversationally, asking questions rather than declaring conclusions.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions can Central Power take within each of its three divisions to improve customer retention, with a bias toward industrial and commercial customers?

categories.name: Sales and General Administration
ideas: Sign multi-year contracts with key industrial and commercial customers to lock in relationships before competitors arrive
Extend credit terms / increase days allowable for accounts receivable for high-value customers
Increase the size of the sales force
Allocate sales staff to specific segments, since the value proposition differs across Industrial, Commercial, and Residential
Assign dedicated account managers to high-value industrial accounts
Reduce or simplify the billing process
Create a website for customers to manage their accounts online

categories.name: Generation and Transmission
ideas: Build substations or add redundancy to improve reliability and power quality for industrial clients
Work with industrial clients on energy efficiency programs to deepen the relationship and raise switching costs

categories.name: Maintenance and Repair
ideas: Prioritize outage repairs by customer value (industrial first) rather than first-come, first-served dispatch
Pre-position repair equipment near clusters of industrial clients to reduce repair response time
Proactively visit industrial clients to inspect their infrastructure or provide engineering advice

recommendation: By investigating the operations of Central Power, we have developed several ideas for strengthening customer retention in the face of competition. No matter which actions are undertaken, there should be a clear bias towards industrial customers, who are more valuable both as a group (58% of revenue) and on a per-customer basis ($1 MM each vs. $480 for residential).
If any of these actions seem attractive to management, we recommend undertaking more detailed analysis to prioritize them by cost, ROI, and feasibility.
risks: Employee, union, or local government resistance to changes in dispatch priority, sales structure, or customer service practices
Actions that are too complex or costly to implement within the one-year pre-deregulation window
Underestimating the speed or sophistication of new entrants once the market opens
next_steps: Analyze costs, potential ROI, and stakeholder effects for each retention initiative identified
Prioritize a shortlist of high-impact, fast-to-implement actions for the pre-deregulation period
Assess employee and union reaction to proposed operational changes and develop a change management plan
